title: The Grand Expedition: the Grand Tour, and the problem they set
summary: They run one machine from every season of the arc in front of a room, submit a season 4 solution to the real grader with everybody watching the verdict screen, and then hand their parents the problem they wrote and grade their submissions against their own test data.
materials: the season 1 badge and the robot, batteries in and both tested the night before
the season 2 adder and the three-mood creature, wired and working
the laptop, with the season 3 shop tally and the closed ledger file already open
the editor and the usaco.org account, logged in before the first guest arrives
your authored problem: the story, the input and output format, the sample, the test data and the reference solution
a second chair at the laptop, for whoever is hunting your problem
an extension lead, and a table where the screen faces the room rather than you
the Error Bestiary and the bug diary, out where people can turn the pages
phone to photograph the four machines and film the verdict screen

steps.title: How the Grand Tour runs
steps.body:
Four machines, one per season, lined up on one table, and you run every one of them yourself. Nobody reaches over your shoulder today, and nobody is allowed to fix anything for you.

The order is the order the seasons happened in, because the tour is the arc and the arc had a direction. The badge and the robot from the forest. The adder and the three-mood creature from the coast. The shop tally with its closed ledger from the mountains. Then a solution from this season, typed in front of them and submitted to the real grader, with the screen facing the room so everybody watches the verdict arrive at the same time you do.

The design loop still runs the hour and today it points somewhere new. Ask: what does each of these four actually prove, and what does it not? Imagine the room in front of the table and pick where each machine has to sit so people can see it working. Plan the order of the four, where the cables go, and what you say while a thing is booting, because the ten seconds of silence while something starts up is the moment a demo falls apart.

One rule for the whole hour, and it is a season 4 rule. Say what each machine cannot do as well as what it can. The badge lights up and it cannot count. The adder adds two small numbers and it cannot subtract. The tally is right about money and knows nothing about whether anyone will buy. Every one of them is honest about its own edges, and saying the edges out loud is what makes the rest believable.

The second half of the hour turns you around completely. The problem you wrote in week 9 gets hunted, at this laptop, by your parents, while you sit beside them as the grader. That half has its own page.

steps.title: For the room only
steps.body:
Everybody else, this step is for you. Hand the device back when you have read it.

They are running this hour. Not helping with it, running it. Four machines and a live submission, in an order they chose, on a table they set up. Three things will make that work and one thing will wreck it.

The thing that wrecks it is a helping hand. If something does not start, if a cable is loose, if a program throws an error in front of you, keep your hands in your lap and say nothing. They have a bug diary two seasons thick and they are faster at this than the fastest of you. Watching a child this age debug in front of an audience is the single best thing on today's programme, and the only way to lose it is to rescue them.

What helps. Ask what a machine cannot do, because they have been told to volunteer that and they will be pleased somebody wanted it. Ask what they would build differently now. And when the grader verdict comes back on screen, read it and react to what it actually says, rather than looking at their face first to find out how to feel.

One thing to know before that screen goes up. The grader is a stranger. It does not know their age, their language or anything about today, and that is exactly why its yes is worth something. If it comes back with something other than a yes, that is not a disaster and it is not a moment to fill with kindness. Ask them what they think happened. They will probably know.

And in the second half they become the examiner. You are going to sit at their laptop and try to solve a problem an actual child this age wrote to catch you. Take it seriously, work it properly, and let them grade you in front of the room.

Five minutes at the keyboard before anybody arrives, and today it is a warm-up rather than training.

Home row first. Then one pass of the words this season made your hands learn in Python: def, return, for, while, in, range, len, int, input, print, open, split. Then one pass of the words it made them learn in the other tongue: include, iostream, using, namespace, std, int, main, vector, cin, cout, return.

Two lists, one pair of hands. That is the whole season in twenty-three words, and this is the last morning of it that anybody sets up for you.

Move any one layer and the program is running in a different world, which is why it worked on my machine is usually true and still not good enough.

steps.title: Why working things break in front of people
steps.body:
Every programmer alive has watched something that worked all week fall over in front of an audience, and the reason is almost never nerves.

The reason is that the environment changed and nobody wrote down how much of it the program was leaning on. A demo does not run on your code. It runs on your code plus a machine, plus whatever is installed on that machine, plus files sitting in particular folders, plus a network, plus a screen at a particular size, plus a handful of small things you did by hand so often that you stopped noticing you were doing them. Move any one of those and the program is genuinely running in a different world.

That is where it worked on my machine comes from, and it is usually a true sentence rather than an excuse. The program did work. It worked in a world that included a file you made last Tuesday and never copied anywhere.

There is a second effect on top of the first. Under an audience, attention narrows onto whatever you are worried about, so the parts you were counting on improvising are exactly the parts that go missing. Which means the fix is not to be braver. The fix is to need less improvisation.

So, engineering, not courage. Write a run sheet: every step in order, including the boring ones like plug this in and open that folder. Do a full dry run on the actual machine, in the actual room, with the actual cables, at least once before the guests are in it. Put everything the demo needs on the machine itself rather than anywhere it has to be fetched from. And decide in advance what you will say if a thing does not start, so the sentence is already in your mouth.

One last piece, which is the only part that is about you. When something does break, say out loud what you think is wrong before you touch anything. It slows you down by four seconds, it is the honest thing, and a room watching somebody reason out loud about a failure never forgets it.

figure.alt: The Grand Tour table, four machines lined up in season order: the season 1 badge and robot from the forest, the season 2 adder and three-mood creature from the coast, the season 3 laptop running the shop tally from the mountains, and the season 4 laptop open on the grader with the screen turned to face the room.

steps.title: The Grand Tour: one machine per season
steps.body:
Run the four, in order, yourself.

The forest. The badge lights up and the robot drives. Say what it senses and what it does with what it senses, and let somebody put a hand in front of it.

The coast. The adder adds two numbers with nothing inside it but switches, and the creature has three moods. Feed the adder a sum in front of them, in binary, and let somebody choose the numbers. Then get the creature into all three moods.

The mountains. The shop tally, running on the real numbers from a real stand, with the ledger closed at the end. Show it a sale, then show it the closing total, and say out loud what that program taught you that had nothing to do with programming.

The desert, and this one is the live part. Open a past problem you have already solved and already had accepted, and say that out loud before you start: this one has been accepted before, so what you are watching is the machine and not a gamble. Read the problem page again in front of them, out loud, because the archive is not all one shape and the page is the authority every single time. Older contests name a pair of files on the page itself and the program has to read and write those exact names. Contests from December 2020 onward take their input from standard input and print to standard output. The page tells you which, and it takes four seconds to check.

Then type the last part, submit, and put the screen where everybody can watch the verdict come back. Say what the verdict means, including that the grader has no idea who typed it. If it comes back as something other than accepted, do not tidy it away: read the message out loud, say what you think happened, and open the file. A wrong answer in front of a room is still information, and it is a better demonstration of this season than a green screen is.
checklist: Every machine was powered up and tested before the first guest arrived, not in front of them
I ran all four myself and nobody else touched a keyboard or a cable
For each machine I said what it cannot do as well as what it can
I read the problem page for its input and output shape before submitting, out loud
The submission happened live with the screen facing the room, and I said what the verdict meant

steps.title: The author's chair, from the other side
steps.body:
Now you swap ends. The problem you wrote in week 9 goes on the table and your parents hunt it while you grade.

What they get: the story, the input format, the output format, and the sample case with its answer. That is exactly what a real contest page gives, and no more.

What they do not get: your test data, your reference solution, or any part of your plan. Those stay closed until you have marked them.

While they work you answer exactly one kind of question, and you say the rule out loud before they start. Questions about what the problem means are yours to answer, because a statement that cannot be understood is your bug and not theirs. Questions about how to solve it get a shrug and nothing else, however much you want to help, and you will want to.

When they hand a program over, you grade it. Run it yourself, on your own test cases, one at a time. Not just the sample, because the sample is the one case you told them about and everything interesting lives in the ones you did not. Go through your cases in the order you built them and say, for each failure, what that particular case was ambushing: the empty one, the biggest one, the tie, the one where everything is the same, the one where the answer is zero.

Then the part that is really the test of your week 9, not of theirs. If a case turns out to be wrong, or a line of your statement turns out to mean two things, or your reference solution disagrees with a correct program of theirs, say so out loud in front of everybody and say which of the three was at fault. Authors find bugs in their own problems all the time. Hiding one is the only version of this that fails.

Finish by showing them the generator: the little script whose only user is a grader, and the reason a problem needs a hundred cases nobody will ever read.
checklist: They got the story, the two formats and the sample, and nothing else
I answered questions about what the problem means and shrugged at questions about how to solve it
I ran their program against every one of my own cases, not just the sample
For every case they failed I said what that case was ambushing
If one of my cases, my statement or my reference solution was wrong, I said so out loud

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt:
Photograph the four machines lined up on the table, in season order, before anybody has touched them.

Then film two moments. The verdict screen coming back on the grader with the room watching it, and a grown-up at your keyboard hunting your problem while you stand behind them saying nothing.

Then attach two files: your reference solution, and the generator script whose only user is a grader.

Then keep the camera rolling for one honest sentence. Of the four machines on that table, which one would be hardest to build again from scratch today, and what does that tell you?

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
